title: Using an oblique pen holder for Copperplate
subtitle: How the angled flange positions the nib at the correct 54-degree Copperplate slant
excerpt: An oblique pen holder angles the nib to the right so that a right-handed writer can achieve the 54-degree slant of Copperplate script without twisting the wrist awkwardly. The flange holds the nib at the correct offset. Loading ink and developing the downstroke pressure take a session or two to become natural.
sourceNotes: Platt Rogers Spencer, Spencerian Key to Practical Penmanship (1866), on pen hold and slant in business penmanship. The oblique holder was a standard piece of commercial penmanship equipment from the mid-nineteenth century and is described in period penmanship manuals held in the Internet Archive collection.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pen holder with a side-mounted metal flange that holds the nib offset to the right. This angles the nib at approximately 55 degrees from the baseline without requiring the writer to rotate their wrist.
The characteristic 54-degree angle of Copperplate letterforms from the baseline, produced by writing with the forearm moving at roughly 45 degrees to the writing line.

content.text: is the standard tool for right-handed Copperplate and Spencerian writing. The metal flange positions the nib to the right of the holder shaft, so the nib tip points at roughly 55 degrees to the right when the holder is held in the natural pen-grip position. items.name: Oblique pen holder
items.notes: The flange is usually adjustable: a small screw or set of curves holds different nib sizes.

items.name: Nikko G nib
items.notes: The standard beginner's Copperplate nib. More rigid than a vintage Hunt 101 or Gillott 303, which makes it easier to control pressure while learning.

items.name: Cartridge paper, 130 gsm
items.notes: For practice. Smooth surfaces (HP watercolour paper or Bristol board) also work and give a cleaner hairline.

items.name: Tracing paper
items.notes: As a hand guard to prevent oils from the writing hand reaching the paper.

items.name: Iron-gall ink or calligraphy gouache
items.notes: Either works for practice. Iron-gall flows well from a Nikko G; gouache in a fine consistency also works.

content.text: Fit the nib into the flange

Slide the nib into the oblique flange so that the vent hole (the small round hole at the top of the nib) sits just inside the flange edge. The flange curves press on the nib shoulders. The nib should be secure but removable with light pressure. If the nib slips, press the flange edges inward slightly with a pair of pliers to tighten the grip.

Hold the oblique holder in the same three-finger grip as a pencil: index finger on top, middle finger below, thumb supporting the side. The holder points back over the right shoulder, not straight up. The wrist rests on the side of the little finger. In this position the nib tip should point at roughly 55 degrees to the right, which is the
. Check by drawing a straight downstroke: it should be at 54 degrees from the baseline, not vertical.

Copperplate is written with flex: light pressure on upstrokes (hairlines) and heavier pressure on downstrokes (shades). The Nikko G produces a hairline at zero pressure and begins to splay to a shade at moderate pressure. Practise the downstroke alone before combining it with the upstroke: start at the top of the x-height, apply pressure as the hand moves down, and release pressure as the nib reaches the baseline. The width of the shade depends on how firmly you press. More than 30 degrees of flex on a modern nib can tear the paper: keep the shade moderate until the pressure response becomes familiar.

items.symptom: The ink blobs at the start of the downstroke
items.cause: Too much ink was loaded on the nib, or the nib was loaded under the tines rather than on the reservoir.
items.fix: Dip the nib to the vent hole only, not past it. Wipe the underside of the nib on the bottle rim before writing.

items.symptom: The upstroke hairline catches and tears the paper
items.cause: The nib is angling slightly into the paper on the upstroke rather than gliding across it.
items.fix: Check that the nib tip is pointing at the correct slant. A nib angled too far to the right on the upstroke digs in. Reduce the holder offset slightly if the angle is consistently wrong.

items.symptom: The holder feels awkward and the grip tenses after a few minutes
items.cause: The holder is gripped too tightly. Calligraphy grip should be light enough to allow the holder to roll slightly between the fingers.
items.fix: Stop, shake out the hand, and resume with a deliberately loose grip. The hand should be able to move the holder freely without squeezing it.
